To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
3-month supplementation with lycopene and/or fish oil did not alter IGF-1 or COX-2 mRNA levels in the normal prostate of men with low-burdens prostate cancer.

compared to placebo, lycopene or eicosapentaenoc acid (EPA)/docosahexanoic acid (DHA) supplementation for 3 months did not significantly change COX-2 or IGF-1 gene expression in men with low-grade prostate cancer.

compared to placebo, 2 months of supplementation with 30 mg of lycopene or 3 g of fish oil did not change IGF- or COX-2 levels, respectively, in the normal prostate of men with low-grade prostate cancer on active surveillance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of lycopenes, a carotenoid found in tomatoes, and fish oils on prostate cancer progression.
the development of a new class of compounds, called "supramolecular polymers" that have the potential for applications in drug delivery and molecular recognition.
the development of new and innovative approaches to the treatment and control of prostate cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
lycopene and/or fish oil supplementation did not alter IGF-1 or COX-2 in men with low burden prostate cancer.
lycopene and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation did not have a significant effect on the expression levels of COX-2 or IGF-1 genes in the prostate tissue of men on active surveillance.
the results of this study did not demonstrate any effect of the supplements in the prostate tissue of men with low-benefit prostate cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of lycopenes and fish oils on the prostate are not as straightforward as we might have hoped.

lycopene and/or fish oil supplementation does not appear to have a major influence on the prostate cancer microenvironment, as assessed by these two genes, at least in men with low-grade disease on active surveillance.
we did not find any evidence for a significant effect of lycopene or omega 3 supplementation on the expression of IGF-1 or COX-2 in men with low-risk prostate cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need more data to determine whether or not these nutrients are helpful for men on active surveillance.
it is not possible to draw definitive conclusions about whether lycopene and omega-3 fatty acids have a direct effect on the prostate gland in men with low burden prostate cancer.

the prostate microenvironment is not a simple model of prostate cancer progression and that there are likely multiple mechanisms by which lycopene and omega-3 fatty acids may impact prostate cancer progression.
